Oct 22 : Meta Platforms has a strong basis for arguing that the $25 billion penalty New Mexico secured this week in a case stemming from allegations the firm mishandled user data should be reduced on appeal, legal experts said.  The judgment was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history. It came after a jury found Meta misled consumers about who had access to their data in the wake of revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm involved in President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users.  New Mexico said state law allowed for a penalty of up to $5,000 for each time someone in the state may have seen an allegedly misleading statement from Meta. Experts said the company would likely argue that Judge Francis Mathew should only have considered people who actually saw the statements.   "The most vulnerable basis on appeal is going to be the question about whether a violation is going to count, even in the absence of any proof that a particular person saw one of these misrepresentations or relied on them to their detriment," said Peter Ormerod, a law professor at Villanova University.

C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. The company is expected to appeal the underlying jury verdict and the penalty. Meta has previously said that it does not sell user data and that New Mexico did not prove any consumer had actually been misled and that a penalty in the billions of dollars would risk violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.  New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday he expected Meta to appeal the judgment and the state stood ready to defend its legal position. He did not immediately respond to a request for further comment. JURY FOUND 43 MILLION VIOLATIONS New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company lied to Facebook users about who had access to their data, how the company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform, and other internal policies.  Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience within New Mexico, the jury said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws. The state had 1.4 million active Facebook users and a population of 2.1 million as of 2020.  Mathew said in his ruling on Wednesday that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount. The state had urged Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, while Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted.  Ormerod said that even if the company's appeals in state courts fail, Meta could argue to the US Supreme Court that the penalty violated its rights under the US Constitution to due process and against excessive fines.  The size of the penalty on its own does not mean it will be overturned, given the New Mexico law allowing for penalties for each willful violation, said Daryl Lim, a professor at Penn State Dickinson Law.  But it seems implausible that Meta was really responsible for so much financial harm, a sign the penalty may be unjust, said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law. "It felt like there was a lot of duplicative counting in the calculations," Goldman said. "How many times can a single person be duped by the same entity?"

Source: Reuters

Oct 22 : Spotify forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates on Thursday, as the Swedish music streaming company bets on its AI-powered features to drive user growth in the crucial holiday season. The company expects operating income of €820 million ($920.53 million), compared with analysts' average estimate of €813.4 million, according to data compiled by LSEG. Shares of the company were last up more than 3 per cent in volatile premarket trading. Spotify offers AI-powered features such as its AI DJ, which curates personalized music mixes with spoken commentary, and prompt-based playlists that let users describe a mood or listening preference to generate tailored selections.

Oct 22 : Customers are increasingly asking where the AI inside their business software was built, SAP's finance chief told Reuters on Thursday, with export controls and Europe's sovereignty debate now shaping decisions once made on price and performance alone. "Could data used by that model be channelled out to end up in places where it shouldn't end up?" Dominik Asam said in the interview, describing a client question SAP regularly hears. It has become an art form to understand companies' precise requirements over technology governance when juggling several AI models, he added. SAP, Europe's most valuable tech company, embeds more than 70 models from various providers into its software that runs accounting and supply chains at many of the world's largest companies, a strategic choice to be agnostic on the market rather than internally build its own models. But for clients, where the AI comes from matters. A US customer may not accept components developed with Chinese models, while others' back-office work, including SAP's own, can run on open-weight software "from wherever it comes from", Asam said.

TOKYO, Oct 22 : Japan's largest labour union group Rengo unveiled a more ambitious wage bargaining policy for next year's annual labour negotiations on Thursday, setting a target centred at a pay hike of 6 per cent while maintaining a minimum benchmark of 5 per cent or more.  The move marks a shift from previous years, when Rengo called for wage increases of at least 5 per cent, as it seeks to reinforce wage-growth momentum after Japanese workers secured average pay gains above 5 per cent for the past three years amid persistent labour shortages. The umbrella group, which represents about 7 million workers, sets wage targets that serve as guidance for its member unions, marking the start of a closely watched bargaining season that will help shape expectations for the Bank of Japan's interest-rate path. The new 6 per cent midpoint target, which includes a 4 per cent base pay increase, is meant to send a message that 5 per cent should be viewed as a floor rather than a target, Rengo said.

The target does not necessarily signal a dramatic increase in actual wage demands, however, as Rengo member unions sought average pay hikes of 5.94 per cent in the 2026 wage round, which resulted in an average increase of 5.01 per cent. RISKS OF INFLATION OVERSHOOT Despite the more assertive target from Rengo, economists expect actual wage settlements in 2027 to remain broadly similar to this year's level of around 5 per cent. "Chronic labour shortages, sturdy corporate profits and a declining labour share of income will justify wage gains broadly comparable to 2026 levels," said Takayasu Kudo, senior Japan economist at Bank of America Securities Japan. While robust pay growth was previously welcomed as a means of lifting inflation towards the central bank's 2 per cent target, stronger wage gains may carry different implications now that the BOJ has shifted its focus to keeping underlying inflation anchored around that level. Wage hikes of around 5 per cent may represent a "sweet spot" for the BOJ as well as workers, said Naoki Hattori, chief Japan economist at Mizuho Research Institute. "Pay hikes larger than that could force companies to pass on labour costs to prices further and risk a wage-price spiral that pushes inflation above the BOJ's 2 per cent target," he said. Japanese wages were stagnant for decades until 2022, when rising raw material costs pushed up inflation and piled pressure on firms to compensate employees with higher pay. Strong wage growth in recent years has helped lift real wages back into positive territory, but Japan still ranks near the bottom among advanced economies in purchasing power parity-adjusted wage comparisons. Seeking to raise Japan's wage levels in international rankings, Rengo also set a medium-term target for the first time, aiming to increase wages by 15 per cent from current levels by 2030. Rengo will formally approve its 2027 wage policy in December, after which individual unions will draw up their demands. Annual wage negotiations typically culminate in March, when major firms respond to union requests.

LONDON, Oct 22 : Flush with money from billionaire donors, Nigel Farage's Reform UK has started hiring staff for a YouTube-based TV channel to bypass established broadcasters and capitalise on fundraising unrivalled by any major political party in Europe. After weeks of bruising headlines over donations and racism that have seen the populist, anti-immigration party led by the veteran Brexit campaigner lose its lead in opinion polls, Reform has started to aggressively spend a bumper £72 million ($96 million) donated by two crypto businessmen. Twelve adverts for media jobs are part of a strategy to regain ground and present the party's message in a more controlled way, according to at least eight party officials. By building on Reform's established YouTube offering, already home to around eight posts a week, the party aims to create a daily channel to try to break the monopoly of an "establishment media" it regards as hostile.

The expansion, enabled by the donations from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo in September, will also help Reform train up more media performers, Gawain Towler, a member of the party's governing board, told Reuters. That would offer respite to Reform's eight lawmakers, who face mainstream media sometimes several times a week each.  PARALLEL WITH TRUMP TV "The media always say they offer a fair hearing to all opinions," said Towler, at Farage's side for more than 20 years. But "when it's Reform, they just want to say we're horrible". About half of the £72 million will cover the running of Reform's headquarters until a national election due by mid-2029, and the funds will also help produce more policy, recruit advisers, expand campaign operations and launch a newspaper with an initial print run of 15 million, the officials said. The TV offering will be similar to US President Donald Trump's Trump TV – a streaming channel airing White House-sanctioned content 24 hours a day. With an estimated initial budget exceeding £10 million and plans for 25 journalists and editors, Reform intends the channel's interviews, documentaries and other content to build on its already well-established social media offering. There is peril. Reform could be forced to hand the funds back if the governing Labour Party changes the rules on donations – something Reform officials say they will contest. But for now, Reform will spend to try to regain ground lost to Labour, under media-savvy new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and the opposition Conservatives, which have in the past few weeks taken the two top spots in opinion polls. Reform is the focus of police and parliamentary investigations over previous funding, including an earlier £5 million to Farage from Harborne, and what the party calls "sting operations". One, broadcast by Channel 4, showed two officials allegedly trying to solicit donations from a foreign-based businessman. Another, broadcast by ITV, showed candidates and councillors making racist, violent and sexist comments. Reform has said its internal review into the two officials had found no breach of electoral law, and Farage told a rally that sometimes people say "unpleasant" and "silly things". Towler and other Reform officials say they do not need to aggressively court donors. Entrepreneurs such as Delo and Harborne offer funds because they believe Reform is the only party that can fix Britain, they say. The two donors have frontloaded their respective £36 million contributions so Reform can prepare for the next election. Announcing his donation, Delo wrote "the party should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government". A source close to Delo, who no longer works in FinTech to concentrate on philanthropy, said there were no strings attached and he was happy with Reform spending the money as it wished. Similarly, Harborne said in his announcement that Reform, as a "start-up party, needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government". He also wrote that he wanted nothing in return.  Reuters could not reach either donor for direct comment. TOP FUNDING SPOT IN EUROPE Reform's record funding not only eclipses Labour and the Conservatives but also tops Germany's centre-right Christian Democratic Union as the largest private annual fundraising haul of any major party in Europe, according to Reuters' analysis of the main European parties' accounts. Reform has raised £87 million from private donors so far this year, with further contributions expected in the coming months, surpassing the previous European record of £86.3 million raised by the CDU in 2024 from donations and membership fees.  Fernando Casal Bertoa, associate politics professor at the University of Nottingham, said UK politics was moving closer to a US-style funding model. "If you give large sums to a party do you really think they won't give you favours or help you?" he added. "It is never for free." Reform officials, and Delo and Harborne, see the cash injection as levelling the playing field with the decades-old Labour and Conservative parties. Harborne has long donated to Reform, and its previous incarnation, the Brexit Party. After contributing more than £228,888 to the Conservatives between 2001 and 2018, Harborne donated about £10 million to the Brexit Party in 2019, according to Electoral Commission data.  It was that year when Towler first "came across" Harborne after the businessman showed interest in the Brexit Party's campaign to stop any attempts to reverse Britain's decision to leave the EU. Harborne's late sister, Katharine, stood as a Brexit Party candidate in 2019. Delo also crossed paths with Farage that year after helping fund the Battle of Ideas festival run by Claire Fox, a former member of the Revolutionary Communist party who joined the Brexit Party in 2019. LABOUR'S THREAT Yet, the scale of Reform's donations has prompted renewed calls for tighter rules in Britain, with Labour threatening to use legislation to introduce retrospective changes that could force Reform to return some of the money. In March, the government announced it would impose a cap of £100,000 on gifts from British donors living overseas. That would apply to donors who move back for a year after they relocate. Electoral records over the summer show Harborne, who moved to Thailand in the 1990s, had registered to vote at a British address. Corporate filings show in early June Delo's place of residence was moved to Britain from Hong Kong. But if the retrospective changes are enacted, it could make all of Harborne and Delo's recent donations ineligible. Reform has described that as a potential "retroactive trapdoor" and a source said if the donations were ruled ineligible, the party could challenge it in court. For now, Reform will spend. "It's a massive game of catch up," said Towler. ($1 = 0.7496 pounds)

Oct 22 : Japanese investors sold foreign bonds for a fifth straight week, their longest selling streak in four years, marking the latest sign of a potential shift in allocation strategy as rising yields at home spur buying in Japanese government bonds. The surge in the benchmark Japanese 10-year bond yield, up over 80 basis points this year, is starting to tease capital home, although recent safe-haven buying has pulled yields away from the three-decade high it hit in October. Japanese investors sold a net 161.6 billion yen ($1.02 billion) of foreign long-term bonds through October 17, the smallest quantum in the streak, alongside 156.9 billion yen of short-term bills, Japan's Ministry of Finance data showed. The pace of selling slowed as US Treasury yields eased from multi-decade highs, as investors sought safety in bonds from the ruction in the stock market over AI worries.

The benchmark 10-year US yield retreated by roughly 27 basis points from a 24-1/2-year high of 5.3645 per cent hit earlier this month. Meanwhile, the 10-year French government bond yield climbed to a 24-year high of 5.022 per cent on Wednesday amid concerns over widespread protests in France. The latest sales brought Japanese investors' total net disposals of foreign long-term bonds over the five weeks to about 3.43 trillion yen, taking year-to-date net sales to 5.18 trillion yen, the largest for the comparable period since 2022. Domestic Japanese banks have led this year's selling, while life insurers have signalled plans to maintain or increase their domestic bond purchases in the second half of the fiscal year. Investor focus this week will be on the investment plans from life insurers, who manage about $2.5 trillion in assets, about a quarter of which is held overseas, according to the Life Insurance Association of Japan. In overseas equity markets, Japanese investors made net purchases of 128.3 billion yen in foreign stocks, marking their fifth weekly net buying in the past six weeks. Meanwhile, foreign investors were net buyers of Japanese long-term bonds for a third consecutive week, purchasing a net 1.45 trillion yen during the week. MANILA, Oct 22 : The Philippine central bank raised its key policy rate by a larger-than-expected 50 basis points (bps) to 5.5 per cent on Thursday, calling it a "decisive" move to combat price pressures while saying it was ready to tighten policy more to cool inflation. "The Monetary Board recognized the need for a strong monetary policy response to broadening price pressures and further upside risks to inflation," the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) said in a statement. The rate hike, the fourth consecutive increase, defied market expectations; all 27 economists polled by Reuters penciled in a quarter-point increase. "Such a decisive response will make monetary policy appropriately restrictive," the BSP said. "This will contain second-round effects and firmly anchor inflation expectations."

The Philippine peso gained after the central bank delivered an outsized interest rate hike on Thursday, but later gave up those gains and drifted back towards a record low as sticky inflation and slowing growth remained key concerns. The peso's recent record low has added to pressure on the BSP to act, with a weaker currency raising the risk of imported inflation in a country that is heavily reliant on fuel imports. The currency has plunged nearly 10 per cent since the beginning of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which sparked a rally in oil prices. After slowing for four straight months, inflation accelerated in September, underscoring the challenge the BSP faces as it keeps monetary policy tight despite weak economic growth in the first half of the year. The BSP kept its average inflation forecast for this year at 6.1 per cent, but raised its projection for next year to 6.0 per cent from 5.4 per cent, citing high global oil prices and the threat posed by El Nino. It expects inflation to return to its target range in 2028 and ease to 3.3 per cent. BSP Governor Eli Remolona said policymakers had room to adjust policy given expectations that the economy would recover, supported by fiscal measures. "We remain open to further interest rate hikes," Remolona said. Lavanya Venkateswaran, senior ASEAN economist at OCBC Bank, expects the BSP to stand pat at its December 17 meeting after Thursday's larger-than-expected increase, but the door to further hikes remains open if core inflation stays elevated in the coming months.

BRUSSELS, Oct 22 : US software company Palantir sought to reassure Europeans that its military AI system used by NATO has no "kill switch", after disruptions to Ukraine's Starlink services heightened concerns about reliance on US tech firms. Ukraine reported last week that its use of military-grade satellite service Starshield, which uses SpaceX's Starlink constellation, had been restricted so that terminals stopped working on fast-moving platforms, hampering tasks such as using interceptor drones to thwart Russian attacks. US and Ukrainian officials and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have offered conflicting explanations for the disruption. But Ukrainian and European officials said they suspected a political motive because the move came after US President Donald Trump demanded Ukraine stop hitting Russian oil refineries. Those suspicions prompted fresh concern among European policymakers that the continent was too dependent on US defence technology that could be cut off, limiting its ability to defend itself.

But Louis Mosley, Palantir’s executive vice president for the UK and Europe, told Reuters on Wednesday that neither the company nor the US could switch off the Maven Smart System AI platform used by NATO’s military headquarters and several European armed forces. “What we have seen in the news over the past few days around Starlink is extremely concerning,” Mosley said in an interview in Brussels. “But as concerns Palantir, I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” he said. “There are no kill switches. There's no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.” MAVEN SYSTEM PROCESSES VAST BATTLEFIELD DATA  The Maven system processes vast amounts of data from satellites, radars and other sensors to give military officers a picture of the battlefield and speed up decision-making. NATO bought Maven for its Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe in 2025 and declared the system had achieved "full technical operational capability" in June this year. But some European NATO members such as Germany and France have not adopted Maven for their own armed forces, citing concerns about relying on a US company amid frequent tensions between Trump and European leaders. In April this year, the head of Germany's cyber command ruled out buying Maven, saying it was "inconceivable" for employees of a private company to have access to the country's national military database. Mosley said it was "entirely at the discretion of the customer" whether Palantir employees were involved in operating the system. Such employees would be citizens of the country concerned and have the required security clearance, he said. "It can absolutely be operated independently of us, and we have many, many customers around the world  —  both actually in the military and in the corporate world  — who do that," he added.

Order intake, the industry's most closely watched metric, was €342.6 million ($385.2 million), rising 17 per cent from the second quarter and 96 per cent from a year ago. Besi is betting on hybrid bonding, a technology that joins stacked chips directly for faster, more energy-efficient connections. Orders for those systems have more than doubled this year compared with all of 2025, it said. "We do not view ASML as a hybrid bonding competitor," CEO Richard Blickman said in the statement, adding that the two Dutch companies were working together to improve how precisely Besi's machines place chips. Besi's shares took a dip last week after research firm SemiAnalysis said that chipmaking equipment maker ASML appeared to be developing a rival hybrid bonding tool. ASML has not confirmed this. Blickman said that, to the best of his knowledge, ASML was interested in "3D transistor stacking inside the chip over the next decade and not in competing with Besi". Investors have also worried that memory makers such as Micron or SK Hynix might be slow to adopt hybrid bonding for high-bandwidth memory, a key component in AI accelerators. Besi shares have roughly halved since a June peak. Analysts polled by LSEG had expected third- and fourth-quarter revenue of €277.3 million and €291.5 million, respectively. It said some customers had asked for deliveries of third-quarter orders to be timed with their production plans for the first half of 2027. ING analyst Marc Hesselink said that stronger orders, hybrid bonding momentum, the ASML clarification and the buyback more than offset the softer guidance, “particularly given the timing-related nature of the shortfall”. LONDON, Oct 22 : Global stocks retreated on Thursday, as tech earnings' optimism provided only fleeting support and was offset by nagging concern over the outlook for AI, while stalemate in the Gulf pushed up oil prices. MSCI's All-World index was set for its largest daily fall in two weeks, down 0.4 per cent, as tech shares from Seoul and Tokyo to Amsterdam and Paris tumbled.  Meta, the first of the so-called AI hyperscalers to publish quarterly results, reported third-quarter revenue late on Wednesday that beat expectations. But any optimism was short-lived, after the company unveiled a plan to issue non-voting stock that revived concern over its mounting capital commitments. "There are lots of cross currents in markets at the moment, which are grappling for a narrative right now," Ben Laidler, head of macro and equity strategy at Bradesco BBI, said.

The Korean won was muted at 1324, after the Bank of Korea left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.00 per cent on Thursday. Gold missed out on safe-haven flows, dropping 1.2 per cent to $4,090 an ounce, while in cryptocurrencies, bitcoin and ether both lost 3 per cent to trade at $82,000 and $2,412, respectively.  (Additional reporting by Jiaxing Li in Hong Kong; Editing by Kate Mayberry, Shri Navaratnam and Susan Fenton)

Oct 21 : Epic Games said its shooter title "Fortnite" will return to Apple's App Store in Australia on Thursday after a federal court ordered the iPhone maker to open up its iOS operating system, having found it violated competition law. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 21 : Tesla is aiming to start selling its Cybercab robotaxis to the public by the end of this year, its engineering chief said on Wednesday, even as the US auto safety agency probes the vehicles that come without manual controls which federal regulations typically require.  The gold, two-seaters – that come with butterfly doors and drive themselves without any steering wheel, pedals or mirrors – are one of the key bets CEO Elon Musk has made in his ambition of turning the EV maker into an AI and robotics company. "As Tesla grows, we'll mainly deliver fully designed autonomous vehicles to our customers and Cybercabs will be the first," Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, told analysts after reporting third-quarter results. "We're trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026," he said. "As we start small this year, and we learn ... about delivery and ownership and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands, we'll continue to scale that."

After years of missed promises by Musk, Tesla started offering paid rides on a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin, Texas, early last month amid a frenzy of fans and social media influencers.  Just hours later, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said it opened an investigation into Cybercabs to assess how Tesla determined the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations. Those regulations, written decades ago for human-driven vehicles, require manual controls and limit commercial deployment of vehicles that are designed without them.  Unlike most other countries, where new vehicle models and technology need regulatory clearance ahead of launch, automakers in the US can deploy them on the public roads by self-certifying that they meet federal standards. NHTSA declined to comment. The agency last month said it was looking into the basis of Tesla's certification of the Cybercab and the extent to which the company determined that certain standards were not applicable to the vehicle. Tesla has until October 30 to respond to the agency.  NHTSA has proposed changes to federal safety standards to allow AVs that are designed without human controls. Until those changes are complete, existing standards remain in force, NHTSA has said.     SCALING THE CYBERCAB "I think the key thing which we are trying to make sure is that we have all the regulatory approvals where we can start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them," Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's head of AI, said on the call. That aside, "scaling would not be that much of a challenge," he said, adding that the Cybercab was "one of the easiest products" to scale in terms of manufacturing. The Cybercab is part of Tesla's robotaxi network that includes autonomous Model Ys, some with human safety monitors. Over time, Tesla intends to make the Cybercab the main driverless vehicle model operating within a larger robotaxi network. Tesla plans to expand the Cybercab service to Dallas next month, Elluswamy said.  The vehicle, however, will mainly be Tesla owned and used for its ride-hailing service, Musk said.

SEOUL: The Bank of Korea kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged on Thursday (Oct 22) but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum. The seven-member monetary policy board at the BOK voted to keep the seven-day repurchase rate at 3 per cent, a decision that was forecast by all 34 analysts surveyed by Reuters. The central bank said that further tightening remains on the table, stating it "will decide the timing and pace of future increases" while assessing inflation, financial stability and domestic economic trends. "The growth rates for this year and next year are expected to be considerably higher than the August forecasts of 3.3 per cent and 2.9 per cent, respectively," the BOK said in a statement, adding a pause on Thursday was needed to evaluate external risks and the lagging effects of its back-to-back hikes in July and August.

It also said that both headline inflation and core inflation for next year will exceed its previous forecasts. "The Bank of Korea left its policy rate unchanged at 3 per cent at today’s meeting, but we doubt this marks the end of the tightening cycle, and have pencilled in one hike for the BOK’s final meeting of the year in November," Gareth Leather, an analyst at Capital Economics said in a note after the decision. The July and August increases were the central bank's first consecutive hikes in more than three years, after which Governor Shin Hyun Song said a gradual pace of tightening was preferred. Shin, however, reiterated at an International Monetary Fund event on Oct 13 that policy would remain restrictive until inflation converges to its target. Headline consumer inflation slowed to 2.9 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent in August, remaining above the bank's 2 per cent target. Exports are powering ahead thanks to global spending on artificial intelligence. Shipments from January to September topped US$800 billion for the first time ever. With growth expected to remain firm and inflation above target, median forecasts in the survey showed the BOK raising its base rate to 3.25 per cent at its November meeting, in line with the BOK's dot plot projection. Shin will hold a news conference at 0210 GMT (10.10am Singapore time).

TOKYO: Major Japanese lenders see increased demand for funds among corporate borrowers compared with three months ago, a survey showed on Thursday (Oct 22), indicating the central bank's recent interest rate hikes have yet to tighten financial conditions. Financial conditions are becoming increasingly important in predicting the timing of the Bank of Japan's next rate hike. The bank has said it will scrutinise how past increases affect corporate funding to assess how close its rate is from a level it deems neutral to the economy. In a survey, that the BOJ conducted over Sep 9 through Oct 13, a diffusion index measuring the ratio of major banks that saw corporate fund demand rise versus those seeing demand shrink stood at +3, compared with -1 in a survey three months earlier. A positive reading indicates more banks saw corporate fund demand increase compared with those that saw demand fall. The BOJ raised its policy interest rate to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent on Sep 18 and signalled a pivot towards a policy focusing on forestalling risk of inflation overshooting its 2 per cent target.
